name: Kombucha ferment

lead: Kombucha ferment is a cosmetic ingredient made by fermenting tea or botanical extracts with a kombucha culture. Marketing links it to antioxidant and soothing effects.
Published work consists of laboratory studies on cells and chemical assays; no human skincare trials were found.

paras: The culture of bacteria and yeast converts sugars into organic acids and alters polyphenols in the extract; in vitro studies report higher antioxidant activity in some fermented extracts.
Topical safety data were not found. Reports of serious adverse events relate mainly to drinking home-brewed kombucha.

lead: Kombucha ferment is a skincare ingredient name for products made by fermenting tea or plant extracts with a kombucha culture (a symbiotic culture of bacteria and yeast, often called SCOBY).[1] Kombucha as a drink is a lightly sweetened fermented black tea, thought to have originated in China.[1]

Laboratory work has fermented botanical extracts with kombucha cultures and measured antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, including a 2023 study of elderberry (Sambucus nigra) fruit ferment on human skin fibroblast cells.[2] No human trials of kombucha ferment as a skincare ingredient were found.

paras: Kombucha is usually made from sweetened tea fermented by a culture whose yeasts commonly include Saccharomyces cerevisiae and whose bacteria include Komagataeibacter xylinus. The finished drink contains organic acids, polyphenols and small amounts of alcohol and has a pH around 3.5.[1]
Its popularity spread from China to Russia and Europe, became a health fad in Japan after a 1974 bestseller, and grew in the United States from the late 1990s.[1]

A 2023 study compared elderberry fruit extract with a version fermented using kombucha culture, assessing chemical composition, antioxidant activity, and effects on lipopolysaccharide-stimulated human skin fibroblasts.[2] A 2022 study found antioxidant activity of kombucha-fermented goji (Lycium barbarum) broth was 16.51% higher than the infusion.[3] These are cell-based or chemical assays.

Wikipedia notes there is no clinical proof of the many health benefits claimed for the drink; a 2003 review by Ernst did not recommend it therapeutically and a 2019 review found one human study. Rare serious adverse events, including contamination and liver or kidney effects in home-brewed versions, have been reported.[1] These concern ingestion, not topical ferments.
No studies found on kombucha ferment applied to skin. Related work is limited to in vitro studies of fermented plant extracts.[2][3]

timeline.event: Japanese kombucha fad follows a bestselling book.[1]
Laboratory studies of kombucha-fermented botanical extracts.[2][3]
